## 1. Story Summary

The 2020 title is often dismissed as a “Mickey Mouse Ring.” But the bubble removed home-court advantage, which normally lets the higher seed host up to four of seven games. Did losing home advantage matter?

Home teams have long had the upper hand in the NBA, winning about 65% of regular-season games in the 1980s. This advantage has been shrinking, falling to a 59% regular-season win rate in the 2010s, but it stayed larger in the playoffs, where home teams won about 63% of games. Part of that playoff edge is simply that the home team is usually the better team. The rest is generally credited to the venue itself: the crowd, familiar surroundings, and an opponent who had to travel.

In the bubble, the designated “home” team was still the higher seed. It just had no building and no crowd. Those teams won only 48% of their playoff games, compared with about 63% in the decade before. With only 83 games the exact figure is uncertain, but it sits well below the usual rate. The Lakers earned the top seed in the West and still won the title without the edge that seed normally buys.

That edge returned along with the fans: home teams won 57% of playoff games in the 2021, when crowds were limited, and 58% from 2022 to 2026. If anything, the bubble made for a harder path for the favourites. It was played at Disney World, but there was nothing Mickey Mouse about it.

## 2. Version A: Scientific Article
*Written for a scientifically literate audience, in the style of a journal article.*

```{r, set up}
#| output: FALSE

library(tidyverse)
library(scales)
library(plotly)
library(readxl)
library(psych)
library(gt)
library(janitor)

```

```{r, loading and processing game data}
#| output: FALSE

#BA Game ID Explained: for example, if an NBA game has the following ID 41900406;
#4: game type (2 = regular season, 4 = playoffs) 19: season start year (2019–20) 00406: game number (always the last 5 digits)

all.games <- read_csv("./Games.csv") |>
  mutate(
    season.yy = (gameId %/% 100000) %% 100, #this allows us to extract the season the game was in
    type.digit = gameId %/% 10000000,       # first digit: 2 = regular season, 4 = playoffs
    game.type  = if_else(type.digit == 2, "Regular Season", "Playoffs"),
    season = if_else(season.yy >= 46, 1900 + season.yy, 2000 + season.yy),
    home.win = winner == hometeamId,
    bubble = between(as_date(gameDate), ymd("2020-07-30"), ymd("2020-10-12"))
  ) |>
    filter(type.digit %in% c(2, 4), #only regular season, and playoffs games survive. All-star = 3, preseason = 1
         season >= 1954) # Regular-season records before 1954-55 are incomplete in the source data
                         # (e.g., 18 of roughly 330 games for 1946-47), so these seasons are excluded.  

```

```{r}
#| label: season-by-season-summary
#| output: FALSE

#season by season summary excluding the bubble games
by.season <- all.games |> 
  filter(!bubble) |>
  group_by(season, game.type) |>
  summarise (n = n(), home.pct = mean(home.win), .groups = "drop")


```

### Long-term trends in home advantage

```{r, first plot, }
#| label: fig-1
#| fig-cap: "Home-team win percentage by NBA season, 1954–55 to 2025–26. Filled circles represent regular season (65,630 games; 288–1,230 per season). Open circles represebt playoffs (4,336 games; 17–89 per season). Lines show locally estimated scatterplot smoothing (LOESS-smoothed) trends. The dotted line marks 50% (no home advantage). Games played in the 2020 Orlando bubble are excluded.Seasons are labelled by start year (e.g., 2018 = 2018–19)"

# Home win % over time, regular season vs playoffs, with a smoothed trend line
# Regular season = filled circle & solid line, Playoffs = hollow circle & dashed line


fig.1 <- ggplot(by.season, aes(x = season, y = home.pct, shape = game.type)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.5, linetype = "dotted",  linewidth = 0.8, colour = "black") +
   annotate("text", x = 1955, y = 0.5, label = "No home advantage",
           vjust = -0.5, hjust = 0, size = 3.5) +
  geom_point() +
    geom_smooth(aes(linetype = game.type), method = "loess", se = FALSE, colour = "black") +
    scale_shape_manual(values = c("Regular Season" = 16,       # filled circle
                                "Playoffs"       = 1)) +     # hollow circle
    scale_linetype_manual(values = c("Regular Season" = "solid",
                                   "Playoffs"       = "dashed")) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(1950, 2020, by = 10)) +
  labs(
    x        = "Season (start year)",
    y        = "Home-team win percentage",
    shape    = "Game type",
    linetype = "Game type") +
  theme(axis.line = element_line(colour = "black"))

fig.1
```


NBA game records go back to the league’s first season in 1946–47, but records before 1954–55 are incomplete in the source data, so our analysis begins there. Across the seven decades since, home teams have held a clear advantage in both the regular season as well as playoffs (fig. 1). During every single regular season, home teams have won more than half of their games, although that edge has been on a downward trend; falling from roughly 73% in the mid 1950s to about 55% by the 2020s. Playoff home teams held an even larger edge, near 85% in the mid 1950s, to almost 65% in the 1970s through the 2000s, before declining in recent seasons. Playoff values vary more from season to season because postseasons include only 17-89 games, compared to the regular season which include 288-1,230 games.

Despite being on a downward trend, the home-court advantage is still a significant factor worth considering.

Home advantage in the playoffs plausibly reflects two kinds of factors. First, the home team is usually the better team, since home court goes to the team with the better regular-season record. Second, there are advantages tied to the venue itself: the home team does not travel, is familiar with its arena and city, has its usual support structure available, and plays in front of its own crowd. In a normal postseason, these factors always occur together, so their contributions cannot be separated.

The 2020 bubble separated tehm. The designated home team was still the higher seed, but every team played at the same neutral site, with no crowds, no travel, and no familiar arena. If team quality drives playoff home advantage, bubble home teams should still have won close to the usual 63% of games. If factors related to the venue drive the advantage, their win percentage should fall toward 50%.

There are many possible contributing factors that could partially explain this advantage. The following are some of the main factors that contribute to the home-court advantage: team with the home advantage is often the better team, having won more games in the regular season. A home ground advantage indicates a team that has won more games, therefore those teams also have an easier schedule during the playoffs (1st seed plays the 8 seed, 2nd seed plays the 7th, etc.). Some secondary advantages that are associated with having a home-court advantage are as follows: They don't have to travel, they are familiar with the arena and the city. Their support structure is available to them given the fact that they are playing in their home.


### The Bubble Experiment


```{r}
#| label: by-period-summary
#| output: false


# Playoff home win % in 5 periods around the 2020 bubble, with 95% CIs
# Only playoff games are used: in the playoffs the home team is the higher seed, which lets the bubble separate team quality from venue effects.

#why choose 5 periods?
#   1. 2010-11 to 2014-15: baseline before the rise of three-point shooting

#   2. 2015-16 to 2018-19: baseline after it; checks whether home advantage had
#                          already changed with playing style before the bubble

#   3. 2019-20 bubble:     neutral site, no crowds, no travel (the test case)

#   4. 2020-21:            home arenas back, crowds limited or absent

#   5. 2021-22 onward:     home arenas and full crowds back



period.levels <- c("2010–11 to\n2014–15",
                   "2015–16 to\n2018–19",
                   "2019–20\n(bubble)",
                   "2020–21\n(limited crowds)",
                   "2021–22 to\n2025–26")

by.period <- all.games |>
  filter(game.type == "Playoffs", season >= 2010) |>
  mutate(period = case_when(
    bubble         ~ period.levels[3],
    season <= 2014 ~ period.levels[1],
    season <= 2018 ~ period.levels[2],
    season == 2020 ~ period.levels[4],
    TRUE           ~ period.levels[5])) |>
  group_by(period) |>
  summarise(n = n(), wins = sum(home.win), home.pct = mean(home.win), .groups = "drop") |>  mutate(se     = sqrt(home.pct * (1 - home.pct) / n),
         lower  = home.pct - 1.96 * se,
         upper  = home.pct + 1.96 * se,
         period = factor(period, levels = period.levels))

```

```{r}
#| label: bubble-tests
#| tbl-cap: "Playoff home win percentage in each period compared with the 2019–20 bubble (two-proportion test)."

# The bubble's row, to compare everything against
bubble.row <- by.period |> filter(period == period.levels[3])

# Test each other period against the bubble
bubble.tests <- by.period |>
  filter(period != period.levels[3]) |>
  rowwise() |>
  mutate(p.value = prop.test(x = c(bubble.row$wins, wins),
                             n = c(bubble.row$n, n),
                             correct = FALSE)$p.value) |>
  ungroup() |>
  select(period, n, wins, home.pct, p.value)

# The p-value for the main comparison (bubble vs 2015-16 to 2018-19), used in Figure 2
p.main <- bubble.tests |> filter(period == period.levels[2]) |> pull(p.value)
p.early <- bubble.tests |> filter(period == period.levels[1]) |> pull(p.value)

# Show the results as a table
bubble.tests |>
  mutate(period   = gsub("\n", " ", period),
         home.pct = scales::percent(home.pct, accuracy = 0.1),
         p.value  = sprintf("%.3f", p.value)) |>
  knitr::kable(col.names = c("Period", "Games", "Home wins", "Home win %", "p (vs bubble)"))

# Do the two pre-bubble baselines differ? (checks the three-point-era question)
base.1 <- by.period |> filter(period == period.levels[1])
base.2 <- by.period |> filter(period == period.levels[2])

p.baselines <- prop.test(x = c(base.1$wins, base.2$wins),
                         n = c(base.1$n, base.2$n),
                         correct = FALSE)$p.value

# --- Post-bubble comparisons ---

# Bubble vs each post-bubble period (already calculated in bubble.tests)
p.bubble.limited <- bubble.tests |> filter(period == period.levels[4]) |> pull(p.value)
p.bubble.full    <- bubble.tests |> filter(period == period.levels[5]) |> pull(p.value)

# Limited crowds vs full crowds: did the return of full crowds make a difference?
limited <- by.period |> filter(period == period.levels[4])
full    <- by.period |> filter(period == period.levels[5])

p.limited.full <- prop.test(x = c(limited$wins, full$wins),
                            n = c(limited$n, full$n),
                            correct = FALSE)$p.value

# Pre-bubble vs full crowds: did home advantage fully recover?
p.pre.full <- prop.test(x = c(base.2$wins, full$wins),
                        n = c(base.2$n, full$n),
                        correct = FALSE)$p.value

# Regular-season seeding games played in the bubble
seeding <- all.games |> filter(game.type == "Regular Season", bubble)
seeding.pct <- mean(seeding$home.win)
seeding.n   <- nrow(seeding)

```


```{r}
#| label: fig-2
#| fig-cap: "Playoff home-court advantage across five periods of the modern NBA, ranging between 2010-11 to 2025-26. Points show the percentage of playoff games won by the home team; vertical bars show 95% confidence intervals (normal approximation); n is the number off playoff games in each period. The  2019-20 season playoffs were played at a single neutral site (the Orlando bubble) without crowds; 2020-21 season playoffs were played in home arenas with limited or no crowds. The dotted line marks 50% (no home advantage) "

fig.2 <- ggplot(by.period, aes(x = period, y = home.pct)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.5, linetype = "dotted", linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_pointrange(aes(ymin = lower, ymax = upper)) +
  annotate("text", x = 1.5, y = 0.5, label = "No home advantage",
           vjust = -0.5, hjust = 1, size = 3.5) +
    annotate("segment", x = 2, xend = 3, y = 0.71, yend = 0.71) +   # horizontal line
  annotate("segment", x = 2, xend = 2, y = 0.71, yend = 0.70) +   # left tick
  annotate("segment", x = 3, xend = 3, y = 0.71, yend = 0.70) +   # right tick
  annotate("text", x = 2.5, y = 0.71, label = sprintf("p = %.3f", p.main),
           vjust = -0.5, size = 3.5) +  
    annotate("segment", x = 1, xend = 3, y = 0.76, yend = 0.76) +   # horizontal line
  annotate("segment", x = 1, xend = 1, y = 0.76, yend = 0.75) +   # left tick
  annotate("segment", x = 3, xend = 3, y = 0.76, yend = 0.75) +   # right tick
  annotate("text", x = 2, y = 0.76, label = sprintf("p = %.3f", p.early),
           vjust = -0.5, size = 3.5) +
  geom_text(aes(label = paste0("n = ", n)), y = 0.33, size = 3.5) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent, limits = c(0.3, 0.8)) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Home-team win percentage (playoffs)") +
  theme(axis.line = element_line(colour = "black"))

fig.2
```

We split the pre-bubble seasons at 2015–16 to check whether home advantage had already shifted with the rise of three-point shooting. The findings suggest no era-specific change in playoff home-court advantage, with a 62.6% home win percentage in 2010–11 to 2014–15 versus 62.9% in 2015–16 to 2018–19 (p = `r sprintf("%.2f", p.baselines)`; @fig-2).

The bubble broke this pattern. Bubble home teams won 48.2% of playoff games (95% CI: 37.4–58.9%), the only period below 50% and significantly lower than both pre-bubble periods (p = `r sprintf("%.3f", p.main)` for each; @tbl-bubble-tests). This is the result predicted by the venue explanation: the home team was still the higher seed, but without its own arena it lost its usual edge. Because the confidence interval includes 50%, the data indicate that home advantage disappeared, not that it reversed.

After the bubble, home win percentages moved back toward pre-bubble levels: 56.5% in 2020-21, when teams returned to their own arenas with limited crowds, and 58.1% from 2021-22 onward. However, neither period differed significantly from the bubble (p = `r sprintf("%.2f", p.bubble.limited)` and p =`r sprintf("%.2f", p.bubble.full)`), so this recovery should be interpreted cautiously.

### Limitations

Several caveats apply. First, the bubble produced only 83 playoff games, so its estimate is imprecise: the 95% CI spans roughly 37% to 59%, and the post-bubble periods could not be statistically distinguished from it. Second, the bubble changed more than the venue. Teams lived in isolation, returned from a four-month long layoff, adn neither team traveled, so the loss of home advantage cannot be attributed to the arena or crowd alone. Third, the 88 regular-season seeding games played in the bubble did not show a comparable decline (55.7% home wins), although this sample is similarly small. Finally, the bubble was a single event and cannot be repeated, so these results should be read as a natural experiment rather tahn a controlled test. What drove the longer-term decline in home advantage shown in @fig-1

(`r scales::percent(seeding.pct, accuracy = 0.1)` home wins across `r seeding.n` games)

### Conclusion
Removing the home venue erased tye playoff home advantage that higher seeds normally enjoy. While the long-standing advantage before and after the bubble remained largely intact. This pattern is more consistent with venue-related factors than wtith team quality alone. For the 2020 title, it suggests that the top seeds, including the champion Los Angeles Lakers, competed without the edge their regular-season records would ordinarily have earned, making their path, if anything, more difficult rather than easier. Because this conclusion rests on a single 83-game natural experiment, it should be treated as suggestive rather than definitive


## 3. Version B: Interactive Explainer

*Written for a general audience, in the style of an online sports explainer.*


### Playing at home has always helped, just less than it used to

Ask any basketball fan and they'll tell you: it's easier to win at home. The numbers agree. For as long as the modern NBA has existed, home teams have won more often than they've lost, but the edge has been slowly shrinking.

*Hover over any dot to see that season's numbers.*

```{r}
#| label: fig-b1
#| fig-cap: "Home teams have always won more than half their games, but the edge is smaller than it used to be. Each dot is one season; the lines show the overall trend."
#| fig-alt: "Line chart of the share of NBA games won by the home team from 1954 to 2025. Both the regular season (grey) and the playoffs (red) start above 70% and decline to about 55%. A red diamond marks the 2020 bubble playoffs at 48%, below the 50% coin-flip line."
#| fig-width: 8

library(plotly)

# Colours: red draws attention to the playoffs, grey keeps the regular season in the background
col.playoffs <- "#B2182B"
col.regular  <- "grey55"

# Season labels like "2019–20" for the hover text
season.label <- function(s) paste0(s, "–", substr(s + 1, 3, 4))

trend.data <- by.season |>
  mutate(type  = if_else(game.type == "Playoffs", "Playoffs", "Regular season"),
         label = paste0(season.label(season), " ", tolower(type), "<br>",
                        "Home teams won ", percent(home.pct, accuracy = 1),
                        " of ", n, " games"))

# The bubble playoffs, highlighted as their own point
bubble.point <- by.period |>
  filter(period == period.levels[3]) |>
  mutate(season = 2019, type = "Playoffs",
         label = paste0("2019–20 playoffs (the bubble)<br>Home teams won ",
                        percent(home.pct, accuracy = 1), " of ", n, " games"))

fig.b1 <- ggplot(trend.data, aes(x = season, y = home.pct, colour = type)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.5, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey40") +
  geom_point(aes(text = label), alpha = 0.35, size = 1.6) +
  geom_smooth(method = "loess", se = FALSE, linewidth = 1.3) +
  geom_point(data = bubble.point, aes(text = label),
             colour = col.playoffs, size = 3, shape = 18) +
  annotate("text", x = 2016, y = 0.43, label = "The 2020 bubble",
           colour = col.playoffs, fontface = "bold", size = 4) +
  annotate("text", x = 1957, y = 0.515, label = "Coin flip (50%)",
           colour = "grey40", hjust = 0, size = 3.5) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("Playoffs" = col.playoffs, "Regular season" = col.regular)) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = percent, limits = c(0.4, 0.9)) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(1960, 2020, 10)) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Games won by the home team", colour = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(legend.position = "top", panel.grid.minor = element_blank())

ggplotly(fig.b1, tooltip = "text") |>
  layout(xaxis = list(showline = TRUE, linecolor = "black", linewidth = 1),
         yaxis = list(showline = TRUE, linecolor = "black", linewidth = 1)) |>
  config(displayModeBar = FALSE)
```


In the playoffs, the edge has usually been bigger. Part of that is simple: in a playoff series, the team with the better record gets to host more games, so the "home" team is usually the better team anyway. The rest comes from the arena itself: the crowd, sleeping in your own bed, and not having to travel.

Normally you can't separate those two things. In 2020, the NBA accidentally did it for us.

### In the bubble, home court vanished

When the pandemic hit, the league finished the 2019–20 season inside a "bubble" at Disney World in Orlando. Every game was played in the same empty arenas. Teams were still labelled "home" and "away", and the better-seeded team was still the "home" team. But there was no home crowd, no home arena and no travel.

The result: playoff "home" teams won fewer than half their games.

```{r}
#| label: fig-b2
#| fig-cap: "Out of every 10 playoff games, how many did the home team win? The bubble is the only period where home teams did worse than a coin flip."
#| fig-alt: "Bar chart of playoff games won by the home team in five periods. 2010–15: 6.3 of 10. 2015–19: 6.3 of 10. 2020 bubble, highlighted in red: 4.8 of 10, below the 50% coin-flip line. 2021: 5.6 of 10. 2022–26: 5.8 of 10."
#| fig-width: 8

# Plain-language labels for each period
plain.levels <- c("2010–15\nBefore the\n3-point boom", "2015–19\nThe 3-point era",
                  "2020\nThe bubble", "2021\nBack home,\nfew fans", "2022–26\nFull crowds")

by.period.plain <- by.period |>
  mutate(plain     = factor(plain.levels[as.integer(period)], levels = plain.levels),
         is.bubble = period == period.levels[3],
         out.of.10 = sprintf("%.1f of 10", home.pct * 10))

ggplot(by.period.plain, aes(x = plain, y = home.pct, fill = is.bubble)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.65) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.5, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey30") +
  geom_text(aes(y = home.pct + 0.03, label = out.of.10),
            vjust = 0, size = 4.5, fontface = "bold") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = col.playoffs, `FALSE` = "grey70"), guide = "none") +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 0.75), expand = c(0, 0),
                     breaks = c(0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75),
                     labels = c("0%", "25%", "50%\n(coin flip)", "75%")) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Playoff games won by the home team") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(), panel.grid.minor = element_blank())
```

Before the bubble, home teams won about 6 of every 10 playoff games, and that held steady even as the game changed with the three-point boom. In the bubble, it fell to fewer than 5 in 10. Being the better team, it turns out, wasn't enough on its own; the home arena was doing a lot of the work.

One honest caveat: the bubble playoffs were only 83 games, so the exact number is a rough estimate. But the drop is big enough that it's very unlikely to be luck alone (see Version A for the statistics).

### Once teams went home, the edge crept back

In 2021, teams returned to their own arenas, mostly with few or no fans. Home teams went back to winning more often, and the numbers have stayed in that range since. With so few games in each period, we can't say for sure how much of the edge has returned. But the one season with no home arenas at all is the one that stands out.

### So, was it a Mickey Mouse ring?

The top seeds in 2020, including the champion Lakers, played the playoffs without the home-court edge their regular seasons would normally have earned them. If anything, that made the title harder to win, not easier.

It was played at Disney World, but there was nothing Mickey Mouse about it.
